Fuel constraints occur when airports’ jet fuel supply cannot keep up with demand, particularly during times of peak demand. There are continued constraints within the fuel distribution system, and the fuel-constrained airports shown in Figure 18 represent a snapshot in time as of 2023. There are airports whose dedicated pipeline from the terminal are operating at capacity and there is limited ability to expand pipeline capacity. Airports with pipeline capacity issues supplement with truck deliveries and tankering during times of peak demand. Airports that receive fuel by truck are impacted by a lack of drivers. National Tank Truck Carriers Inc. reported in May 2021 that the previous 2 years saw a 42% decline in qualified driver applicants and an overall decline of 23% of drivers (National Tank Truck Carriers 2021). Constrained airports information was provided to the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) by Airlines for America in September 2023. 2.1.3.1 Airport Infrastructure All commercial airports have on-site fuel storage in an area called the tank farm. A tank farm comprises multiple interconnected pieces of equipment designed to safely receive, store, and dispense fuel to a hydrant system or truck delivery to aircraft (Moriarty and McCormick 2024). Generally, airports own the tank farm and lease it to an airline fuel consortium or fixed-based operator who manages it. Smaller airports may operate differently, where the airport operates the fuel system or hires a third party to do so. Because SAF/Jet A blends are delivered from terminals via the same pipelines and trucks used for Jet A, airports do not need to make any changes to their airport tank farms or procedures to receive SAF/Jet A blends. The purpose of airline fuel consortiums, common at U.S. airports, is to pool resources and ensure quality and timely delivery of jet fuel to all airlines through shared infrastructure. The airline consortium model allows airlines to source fuel from multiple fuel producers. Airline fuel consortiums do not buy or sell fuel, but act as the operator of the fuel infrastructure. Airlines are responsible for purchasing fuel and ensuring quality. The consortium may directly operate the infrastructure system or contract out operations to a third party.
